title: Lesson 4: Avoiding Gossip, Retaliation and Taking Sides
summary: Gossip, retaliation and taking sides can turn a small disagreement into a team-wide problem. Support fair solutions, not workplace divisions.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Gossip, rumours, retaliation, cliques and fair professional support

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Two employees have a disagreement about shared responsibilities.
Instead of resolving the issue directly, one employee begins telling colleagues: "She thinks she's better than everybody. You should see how she behaves."
Another employee responds: "I've noticed that too. I don't even like working with her."
Soon, several employees begin discussing the disagreement. Some support the first employee. Others support the second.

The original issue becomes less important than the growing division within the team. One employee begins refusing to assist the other. Another deliberately excludes her from relevant work conversations.
What began as a disagreement between two people has now affected the entire workplace.
Gossip, retaliation and taking sides can turn a small conflict into a larger team problem.

sections.title: 2. What is workplace gossip?
paragraphs: Workplace gossip involves unnecessary discussion of another person's private affairs, mistakes, relationships or behaviour, especially when the information is unverified, confidential or shared to ridicule or undermine the person.
Not every discussion about another employee is gossip.
Reporting misconduct, raising a genuine concern or sharing necessary operational information through an appropriate channel can be legitimate.
The purpose, accuracy, confidentiality and relevance of the communication matter.
list: Discussing a colleague's private concerns without permission.
Sharing someone's mistake with employees who have no legitimate reason to know.
Speculating about why an employee received a correction.
Making negative comments about colleagues behind their backs.

sections.title: 3. Why gossip is harmful
paragraphs: Employees should not turn speculation into workplace information.

sections.title: Example — an unverified dismissal rumour
paragraphs: A therapist tells colleagues: "I heard the receptionist is about to be dismissed." The information is unverified.
The receptionist hears about the rumour and becomes distressed.
Even if the rumour is false, the damage to workplace trust may already have occurred.

sections.title: 4. What is retaliation?
paragraphs: Retaliation occurs when someone deliberately punishes, threatens or disadvantages another person because of a complaint, disagreement, report or other protected or legitimate action.
Employees should not punish colleagues for raising legitimate workplace concerns.
list: Refusing necessary work cooperation because someone reported a concern.
Deliberately excluding an employee from relevant work information.
Threatening a colleague for speaking to a supervisor.
Spreading damaging rumours after a disagreement.
Deliberately interfering with someone's assigned work.
Intimidating someone who raised a genuine concern.

sections.title: Example — a reported handover problem
paragraphs: A therapist reports a repeated handover problem to the supervisor.
The colleague involved becomes angry and says: "Since you reported me, don't ever expect me to help you again."
If she deliberately withholds necessary cooperation, this may constitute retaliation.

sections.title: 5. What does taking sides mean?
paragraphs: Taking sides occurs when employees become personally involved in another disagreement by supporting one person against another without fairly considering the facts.
Remaining neutral does not mean ignoring serious misconduct.
Employees should report threats, harassment, safety concerns or other serious incidents appropriately.
Fairness means considering the facts, not pretending every action is equally acceptable.
Friendship should not determine what is right or wrong.

sections.title: Example — supporting a friend automatically
paragraphs: Two employees disagree about an appointment. A third employee says: "I don't care what happened. She's my friend, so I'm supporting her."
This is not an objective response.

sections.title: 6. The difference between supporting a colleague and taking sides
table: Helping someone access the right reporting channel

sections.title: 7. Why employees form cliques during conflicts
paragraphs: Friendships are not prohibited. However, friendships should not interfere with professional fairness, communication or teamwork.
list: Develop resentment toward other team members.

sections.title: 8. What to do when someone invites you into gossip
paragraphs: An employee says: "Come, let me tell you what happened between those two."
You can respond: "I'd rather not discuss their disagreement without the full facts. If there's a genuine concern, it should be addressed appropriately."
Another possible response: "I don't think discussing this among ourselves will help. They may need to speak with the supervisor."
You do not need to insult the person spreading gossip. You can simply refuse to participate.

sections.title: 9. What to do if someone asks you to take sides
paragraphs: A colleague says: "You're my friend. Tell me you're supporting me against her."
A professional response would be: "I care about you, but I don't want to judge the situation without understanding what happened. I think the issue should be resolved fairly."
Supporting a friend does not require defending inappropriate behaviour.

sections.title: 10. When a disagreement involves close friends
paragraphs: Suppose two employees are close friends. One of them behaves disrespectfully toward another colleague.
The friend should not automatically excuse the behaviour.
She may say privately: "I understand you're upset, but I don't think the way you spoke to her was appropriate. You can raise the concern without insulting her."
This demonstrates genuine support without encouraging misconduct.

sections.title: 11. Protecting confidentiality during conflict
paragraphs: Relevant information should be shared only with people who have an appropriate reason to receive it.

sections.title: 12. Lesson 4 case study
paragraphs: A therapist reports a colleague's repeated failure to replenish room supplies.
The colleague becomes angry and tells other staff members not to assist the therapist who made the report.
Expected lesson: Reporting legitimate concerns should not lead to punishment, gossip or workplace exclusion.
list: Was reporting the repeated concern necessarily wrong?
What behaviour may amount to retaliation?
Why should colleagues avoid taking sides?
How should management address the concern?
How can professional cooperation be restored?

sections.title: 13. Practical exercise: Choose the professional response
table: Avoid repeating it and seek appropriate clarification if necessary
A colleague asks you to support her against another employee
Encourage a fair review of the facts
Do not excuse the insult because of friendship
Someone threatens an employee for reporting a concern
Report the threat through an appropriate channel
Employees discuss a confidential complaint in a group chat
Stop unnecessary sharing and redirect the matter appropriately

remember: Do not allow friendship, anger or loyalty to turn you against another employee. Avoid gossip, refuse retaliation and support fair solutions rather than workplace divisions.
